headlines.full_text: Keiko Fujimori sworn in as Peru president after narrow election win Fujimori takes office promising an iron-fisted crackdown on crime, as critics fear a return to her father's tactics. Save Share Keiko Fujimori has been sworn in as Peru’s president afternarrowly winningan election dominated by voters’ fears over soaring crime and despite lingering divisions over the legacy of her strongman father, Alberto Fujimori. The conservative 51-year-old defeated left-wing rival Roberto Sanchez by fewer than 50,000 votes in June’s run-off after losing three previous presidential bids. She becomes Peru’s ninth president in a decade, taking office with a promise to restore stability after years of political turmoil that have seen a string of presidents removed, resign or replaced before finishing their terms. “I swear … that I will faithfully carry out the duties of president of the republic,” Fujimori told Congress during her inauguration ceremony on Tuesday. Fujimori’s Fuerza Popular is the largest bloc in Congress. Together with its main right-wing ally, it will hold half the seats in the newly installed Senate, making it harder for her to be removed as president, although right-wing parties still fall short of the majority needed to push through her agenda. headlines.full_text: Keiko Fujimori sworn in as Peru’s president The inauguration ceremony was attended by the presidents of Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile BUENOS AIRES, July 28. /TASS/. Keiko Fujimori has been sworn in as Peru’s first female president. The ceremony was broadcast onPeru TV. "I, Keiko Fujimori, swear that I will faithfully fulfill the duties of president entrusted to me for the term of 2026-2031," she said. The inauguration ceremony was attended by the presidents of Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile - Javier Milei, Rodrigo Paz, and Jose Antonio Kast. Keiko Fujimori, 51, is the daughter of Peru’s ex-President Alberto Fujimori, who occupied office from 1990 to 2000 and was sentenced to 25 years behind bars for human rights violations. Before winning the 2026 presidential election, she vied for the office three times - in 2011, 2016, and 2021, but each time lost in the runoff election. Her political program includes the use of military intelligence and other army units to fight against violence and organized crime, as well as the transfer the control over the penitentiary system to the military for the period of its reforming. He economic plan envisages encouraging the development of production sectors, including the mining and processing industries, and energy to boost their competitiveness, as well as creating new jobs, and supporting businesses. She also stands for closer cooperation with the United States and right-wing leaders of regional countries.

"Obviously, they are seeking to destabilize the situation in our country, create negative moods," he noted. "This manifests itself in various ways - even in posts on a number of social media platforms," Medvedev said, citing as an example pseudo-campaigning encouraging people to enlist as contract soldiers "without waiting" for the draft. headlines.full_text: European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled A blaze near Bordeaux has torn through more than 162 sq miles (420 sq km) in less than four days, while the Madrid region is seeing its worst fires ever. Wildfires are tearing through France and Spain, forcing more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes. France has seen its worst fires in two decades, while officials in the Spanish capital Madrid say they are the worst the region has ever experienced. It follows a sweltering summer of heatwaves across Europe that have seen temperatures soar above 40C (104F) in many places. Wildfires in the regions outside Madrid have burned about 254 sq miles (660 sq km) since 1 July, authorities estimate - an area larger than the city itself. In France, the worst affected area is Gironde, around the city of Bordeaux, where more than 200,000 people have been forced from their homes. The blaze has spread rapidly, tearing through forests and fields in France's famous wine region, and burning more than 162 sq miles (420 sq km) in less than four days - an area roughly four times the size of Paris. It is now just nine miles (15km) from the south of Bordeaux. The fires have also threatened a number of sensitive military and industrial sites in the area, including facilities that work on French ballistic missiles, rocket motors, and the processing of hazardous chemicals. The fires have become so extreme they have created their own giant fire thunderstorm. A rare weather event, storms like these are formed when heat from the wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly, carrying smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere. headlines.full_text: Europe is battling the worst wave of forest fires in its history Raging fires in the forests of several countries in southern Europe, leaving a crisis that is now out of control. Large areas of France, Spain and Italy are witnessing an unprecedented wave of fires. More than 300,000 people in France and Spain were forced by fires to evacuate their homes in evacuations that the French Interior Ministry described as the largest in peacetime. The Spanish authorities also imposed strict restrictions on traffic in the vicinity of the town of Cebreros, located west of Madrid and in the province of Avila, and closed the roads leading to it due to the fire approaching the traffic hubs and the continuation of firefighting operations. Amid European officials' warnings of the outbreak of new fires due to high temperatures and low humidity, and calls to adopt a comprehensive national climate charter, Europe stands unable to confront the deluge of fires that send a message that climate change is a real danger, and that denying it may prevent us from anticipating the scale of the challenge facing the world. Report: Shaima Abu Zaid Reading: Fadel Abu Al-Hassan Save Share
headlines.llm_reasoning: The article exaggerates the severity of the forest fires and their connection to climate change to provoke a sense of urgency and alarm.

Over 9,000 firefighters, troops, police, and other emergency personnel have been mobilized to battle the blaze, backed by dozens of aircraft and hundreds of vehicles. However, dry conditions and another approaching heatwave have complicated their efforts. Authorities say this year’s wildfires are among the worst on record. Spain’s response has been further hampered by its inability to deploy its former fleet of Russian-made Kamov Ka-32 helicopters. The aircraft are considered particularly effective for wildfire missions due to their large water capacity, maneuverability, and ability to operate in extreme heat and difficult terrain. Previously used under contracts with Spain’s national and regional authorities, the fleet has remained grounded under the EU sanctions regime that was imposed against Russia following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. headlines.full_text: Deadly French wildfires threaten missile plants, nuclear sites as fourth heatwave looms Missile factories and nuclear research sites near Bordeaux face evacuation as wildfires scorch over 104,000 acres in France's worst blaze on record. Wildfires are sweeping across Spain and France, forcing more than 250,000 people to evacuate. One blaze is threatening France's famed Bordeaux wine region, while Spain has declared a national emergency. France has deployed the military, and the Tour de France has been shortened as firefighters battle the massive blazes. Massive wildfires sweeping through southwestern France are threatening key defense and nuclear sites near Bordeaux, forcing evacuations and emergency measures at missile factories, military research facilities and aerospace plants, according to reports. The escalating blazes come as France braces for its fourth major heat wave of the year Tuesday, with soaring temperatures and arid conditions increasing pressure on crews battling massive wildfires near Bordeaux, according toReuters. Temperatures in the French region were forecast to reach 91 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius), about 13 degrees (7 degrees Celsius) above normal, according to theReuters Climate Monitor. headlines.full_text: As the US pauses the war with Iran, is Trump really running out of weapons? The US has fired thousands of hard-to-replace missiles during its war with Iran. We unpack whether its "arsenal of freedom" is perilously low. When US President Donald Trump took the stage earlier this month at the Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit, flanked by the CEOs of some of America's largest defence firms, he had one message in mind: build more weapons, and build them faster. "We have the best quality in the world," Trump told the armsmakers gathered at the US Army War College, with 'Secretary of War' Pete Hegseth at his side. "But we need a little more speed." The Trump administration framed the summit as part of a two-pronged approach to revitalise American industry and bolster US warfighting capabilities and, in Hegseth's words, its "arsenal of freedom". Largely unspoken, however, was the vast expenditure of sophisticated and difficult-to-manufacture weapons used during nearly 40 days of intense combat operations in Iran during Operation Epic Fury earlier this year and tit-for-tat strikes that have taken place since. So far, the US government says the war has cost $37.5bn (£28bn), and the vast majority of that has been spent on munitions. By the time a tenuous ceasefire took effect on 8 April, US forces had struck over 13,000 targets across Iran, according to the White House. American air defences intercepted over 1,700 Iranian drones and ballistic missiles over the same period. Now, the US has paused its strikes on Iran to allow negotiations to go ahead. headlines.full_text: Iranian Parliament passes legislation defining crimes of foreign aggression TEHRAN — Iranian lawmakers have overwhelmingly approved key provisions defining and criminalizing acts of foreign aggression against the country's national sovereignty and territorial integrity. TEHRAN — Iranian lawmakers have overwhelmingly approved key provisions defining and criminalizing acts of foreign aggression against the country's national sovereignty and territorial integrity. During a parliamentary session focused on a single-urgency bill aimed at combating international crimes, representatives ratified Articles 7 and 8 of the draft law. The legislative measure establishes a firm judicial mandate targeting political officials and military leaders who plan, initiate, or execute aggressive actions against the nation's independence. Under Article 7 of the law, any act of aggression, planning, or preparation directed against the country’s sovereignty or political independence—regardless of whether a formal declaration of war has been issued—is classified as a major crime. Those found guilty, including high-ranking commanders and directors, face Grade 1 imprisonment alongside substantial monetary fines. The newly approved legislation outlines six specific categories of illegal foreign aggression: direct armed invasions, military occupations, or forceful territorial annexations; unprovoked bombardment or missile strikes against national territory; naval blockades targeting ports or coastal waters; attacks against land, sea, or air defense forces; misuse or unauthorized extension of foreign military presence beyond contractual agreements; and permitting national territory to be utilized by a foreign state for launching attacks against a third party. headlines.full_text: Is Israel really isolated? Polls and diplomacy point in opposite directions Trump says the Saudi Arabia nuclear deal hinges on joining the Abraham Accords, as experts debate whether Israel faces isolation or expanding ties. Richard Goldberg argues that Israel’s strategic relationships are expanding even as opposition grows among Democrats, international institutions and parts of Western public opinion. President Donald Trump predicted in recent days that additional countries would soon join the Abraham Accords, renewing debate over whether Israel is becoming increasingly isolated or continuing to expand its most important strategic relationships. "The Abraham Accords have been, I think, a tremendous success," Trump said during a Tuesday Oval Office meeting withLebanese PresidentJoseph Aoun. On the surface, the meeting carries all the hallmarks of an extraordinary victory lap. Less than five months ago, the US and Israel embarked on a joint military campaign against Iran — an unprecedented operational campaign that decimated key Iranian military command centres, and resulted in the death of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Yet behind the closed doors of the West Wing, the alignment between Trump and Netanyahu has fractured under the weight of competing priorities, broken trust, and drastically opposing visions for West Asia’s post-war order. Today’s summit — the first face-to-face encounter between the two leaders since the outbreak of the Iran war — comes at a delicate juncture. headlines.full_text: Trump administration bans new Chinese humanoid robots The US and China are locked in a race to the lead the world in robotics and artificial intelligence. The Trump administration on Tuesday announced a ban on new foreign-made humanoid robot imports to the US over "unacceptable risks" to the country's national security. The move applies to advanced robots - including humanoid and four-legged machines. Many of them are made in China, which is locked in a race with the US to develop robotics and artificial intelligence (AI). The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) also banned the import of power inverters - a device used in data centres and solar panels - which it said could also pose a risk to the US economy. FCC chairman Brendan Carr said the agency was doing its part "to secure America's critical supply chains". The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in Washington as well as major Chinese robot manufacturers Unitree, UBTech and AgiBot. The FCC has added the items to its Covered List - a register of goods and services that are deemed a risk to US national security. The ban applies to new foreign-produced advanced robotic devices and power inverters and does not prevent the sale or import of any existing models that had been previously authorised by the FCC. The FCC cited concerns that the use of foreign-made inverters could allow overseas firms to turn them off, steal data, facilitate remote access and surveillance by "foreign government actors, or be otherwise exploited through a cyberattack." At 34, Captain Bustamante is the oldest among them and moves like the special forces officer he used to be. With the sun setting, he leads his team into a hardscrabble neighbourhood where windows are sealed off behind metal grills, and lips are sealed by fear. This is the heart of gangland, controlled by a group called Los Aguilas (Spanish for The Eagles). I ask what happens if local people speak out against the gangs. "They kill them," the captain replies. "So that's why they never say nothing." He's heading for an abandoned house where he believes weapons have been hidden (gunmen don't keep their guns at home). headlines.full_text: Sudan civil war: Civilians used as 'human shields' The situation in the besieged city of El Obeid in Sudan is worsening by the day, with rights organizations warning of mass atrocities. Children are traumatized and do not dare go to school. Flattened houses and rubble where a school once stood: These are the scenes that have appeared in footage of the Sudanese city of El Obeid published by Ayin Network, a nonpartisan Sudanese media outlet. Drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have caused enormous damage to civilian infrastructure, including power grids, transformers, water treatment plants, schools, universities and hospitals in the capital of North Kordofan. The local population is struggling to survive,according to Ahmed Awad, project manager for the UK children's rights organization Plan International, and a native of El Obeid. The city — whose population previously numbered half a million but has now become home to several hundred thousand internally displaced persons (IDP) — is under siege, he added. There is a shortage of medical supplies as well as food and safe, clean water, and Awad said he saw long queues of IDPs at just one water pump: "Sometimes you can spend all day to get one liter of water for two or three days." He added that a drone had hit a primary school and killed three children, which had caused trauma among other children, many of whom no longer dared go to school. "One of the mothers said three of her children cannot sleep because always they are in fear of something happening again," he said, adding that Plan International tried "to provide psychosocial support" for people scared of drones that could hit a classroom at any time. headlines.full_text: What will it take to stop the conflict in Sudan? The army says it's retaken a key highway linking Khartoum to El-Obeid. The army says it’s retaken a key highway linking Khartoum to El-Obeid. Three years of fighting between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have devastated Sudan. The conflict has caused the world’s largest humanitarian crisis, displacing more than 13 million people and killing tens of thousands of civilians. More than half of the population needs aid. The health system is in ruins, and millions of children are out of school. Both sides have been accused of war crimes and other abuses. Recent fighting has centred around the city of el-Obeid, under siege by paramilitaries. The army has retaken a main highway linking it to the capital, which could weaken the RSF. But hundreds of thousands of people trapped there are still at risk. So, what will it take to stop the conflict? headlines.full_text: New German envoy may hinder dialogue with Moscow by talking of demands for Russia — MFA Earlier, the German diplomatic mission published a video on its Telegram channel in which von Goetze confirms that he has arrived in Russia and has assumed his duties MOSCOW, July 28. /TASS/. The statements of the new German ambassador to Russia, Clemens von Goetze, regarding demands for Russia may lead to his dialogue with Moscow failing to develop, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has stated. "The new German ambassador, having barely arrived in Russia, attempted to deliver a public greeting by stating that he would demand something from the Russian government. This was a clear false start. With such an understanding of the purpose of his diplomatic mission, the German diplomat's dialogue in Moscow will not succeed," the diplomat said on her Telegram channel. "He also said that Russian citizens had given him a warm welcome. Given that he does not speak Russian, we would ask him not to be deluded: perhaps you misunderstood Russian idiomatic expressions. Therefore, we strongly recommend that the ambassador not attribute his fantasies to Russian citizens," Zakharova added. Earlier, the German diplomatic mission published a video on its Telegram channel in which von Goetze confirms that he has arrived in Russia and has assumed his duties.
headlines.llm_reasoning: The Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova attributes the German ambassador's 'demands' to Russian citizens, implying that they are somehow responsible for the ambassador's actions.

headlines.full_text: UN sounds warning as refugee convention turns 75 UN sounds warning as refugee convention turns 75 The right to asylum is coming under increasing political strain across the world, the UN's refugees chief said Tuesday as he marked the 75th anniversary of the Refugee Convention. At the United Nation's Palais des Nations in Geneva where the convention was opened for signature on July 28, 1951 UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih urged the world to move from managing sky-high displacement to seeking to resolve it. "We gather at a time of increasingly politicised debates about refugees and asylum," said Iraqi ex-president Salih, himself a former refugee. "Too often, people forced to flee become scapegoats for wider social, economic and political anxieties. Too often, refugees are portrayed as burdens or threats rather than as fellow human beings." Some 117.8 million people worldwide were forcibly displaced from their homes at the end of 2025, according to UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, down slightly from 2024's record 123.2 million. Last year's drop was the first in a decade, as conflicts in Iran and Lebanon spurred many refugees hosted there to return home, often under risky circumstances, including to Syria and Afghanistan. In a message, UN chief Antonio Guterres said that in the aftermath of World War II, states made a solemn promise that no-one fleeing persecution would be returned to a place where their life or freedom would be threatened on account of their race, religion, nationality, social group or political opinion. headlines.full_text: 'Life-threatening situation': 13 Indian seafarers stranded at Ukraine's Black Sea port amid drone attacks The appeal comes a day after India raised concerns with Ukraine over the safety of Indian crew members operating in the Black Sea. Thirteen Indian seafarers are among 15 crew members stranded aboard a cargo vessel at Ukraine’s Chornomorsk port, where continuing drone and missile attacks have left them trapped in what the Forward Seamen’s Union of India (FSUI) described as a “life-threatening” situation. In an urgent appeal posted on X, the union said the vessel, MV AMIR1, remains docked at the Black Sea port as hostilities continue in the surrounding area. According to the FSUI, the crew has been forced to remain on board as repeated drone and missile strikes continue near the vessel. “MV AMIR1, currently at Ukrainian port Chornomorsk with 15 crew on board, including 13 Indian seafarers, is trapped in a terrible and life-threatening situation,” the union said. It added that the sailors were living under constant fear of being caught in an attack. “Repeated drone and missile attacks are being attempted in the immediate vicinity of the vessel. The crew is living under constant fear of a direct hit at any moment,” the union said. The seafarers’ body appealed to the shipowners, the vessel’s flag state, relevant authorities and the Government of India to intervene immediately and ensure the crew’s safe evacuation. “We urgently appeal to all concerned authorities, shipowners, flag state, and the Government of India to immediately secure their safety and arrange prompt repatriation,” the union said. The missing crew members have been identified as Chandra Ram Dubey and Deepak Kumar Gupta. According to the DMA, the vessel came under attack by three drones on Saturday evening. During the assault, the two Indian seafarers reportedly jumped into the Black Sea in an attempt to save themselves. Their whereabouts have remained unknown since then. The remaining seven crew members, including two other Indian nationals, along with a pilot, were safely evacuated to shore by the Ukrainian Coast Guard. The DMA said a Search and Rescue (SAR) operation was launched immediately after the incident but has been temporarily suspended due to the continuing threat of drone attacks in the area. The search will resume once the security situation improves. The incident comes amid an increase in attacks on commercial vessels operating in the Black Sea. Satirical posters mocking India's legislative, executive and judiciary were plastered on the walls, and the pavement was sprayed with sometimes "vulgar" graffiti mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The German government has ordered a review of the country’s terrorism laws and judicial processes following the Berlin Pride attack, which left one person dead and 29 others injured. The man who carried out the attack, Abdul Ballout, was convicted of preparing a serious act of violence but avoided prison after the judge handed him a suspended sentence, replacing prison time with probation. He was inspired by the Islamic State and had unsuccessfully attempted to travel to Syria to join the terrorist group. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said it was incomprehensible that Ballout had been handed a suspended sentence, “given the level of danger involved in this case”. “We know that he committed a large number of offences, that he sympathised with terror, that there was also a conviction that was suspended on probation, and that the public prosecutor’s office lodged an appeal against it. They were believed to be the last of their kind. Experts at Chester Zoo said they had to brave treacherous conditions and climb cliffs to return them to their natural home, which is part of the Madeira archipelago in the Atlantic ocean. The Madeira government had asked the Chester Zoo experts to help with the snail conservation. The conservationists had scramble from the water up a cliff face in the dark to find cracks in the rocks where the snails could be safely left. Tamas Papp, assistant team manager for invertebrates at Chester Zoo, said: "We knew we had one shot to save them. "If we missed this chance, that was it: they were gone." Papp added: "It might be the trickiest reintroduction we've ever done. "We had a short window due to rough weather, and there's no jetty on the island. "We had to jump straight into the water, climb out, put helmets and harnesses on, and start scrambling up the cliff face." The snails, which measure no bigger than a third of an inch or 8mm in size, are important as they eat vegetation and enrich the soil. They will be monitored as they settle back into the wild. Iranian Minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri made the proposal during talks with Ho Min, head of the Korea Heritage Service, who welcomed the initiative, IRNA reported on Monday. The meeting took place after UNESCO's World Heritage Committee on Sunday inscribed the serial property of “Alamut Castle and Related Fortifications” as Iran's 30th tangible cultural property on the World Heritage List. The newly listed property comprises seven castles and fortifications across the eastern and western Alamut valleys and the southern slopes of the Alborz Mountains in Qazvin province. headlines.full_text: Why the US is reviving PAC-2 Patriot missiles after 30 years amid a growing interceptor crunch The move marks a shift in US missile procurement as Washington looks for a faster and more affordable way to replenish its depleted inventories while expanding production of newer interceptors. Facing growing pressure on its missile stockpiles after conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and across West Asia, the US Army has placed its first domestic order for Patriot Advanced Capability-2 (PAC-2) Guidance Enhanced Missile-Tactical (GEM-T) interceptors in more than three decades, according toThe Times of India. The $441 million contract marks a significant shift in US air defence procurement, with Washington turning back to the older but cheaper PAC-2 interceptor to replenish rapidly depleting inventories while expanding production of the newer PAC-3 missile. headlines.full_text: Why is Johnson & Johnson paying $5.5 billion over baby powder lawsuits? Johnson & Johnson has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5 billion to settle around 76,000 lawsuits alleging its talc-based baby powder caused ovarian cancer. Here's how the landmark settlement came about, why the company still denies wrongdoing, and what it means for one of America's biggest corporate legal battles Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5 billion to resolve the overwhelming majority of lawsuits alleging that its talc-based baby powder and other talc products caused ovarian cancer, marking what could be the final chapter in one of the largest and longest-running product liability battles in United States corporate history. The proposed agreement, announced on July 27, covers approximately 76,000 existing claims pending in US federal and state courts, representing nearly all of the remaining ovarian cancer-related talc litigation against the healthcare giant. Although Johnson & Johnson continues to deny that its talc products are unsafe or contain asbestos, it says the agreement is intended to end years of costly litigation and allow the company to focus on its core healthcare business. However, the settlement will only become legally binding if 95 per cent of eligible ovarian cancer claimants in state and federal courts agree to participate. Instead of continuing to fight thousands of individual lawsuits — or attempting to resolve the claims through bankruptcy proceedings — the company has negotiated a direct out-of-court agreement with plaintiffs’ lawyers. Under the framework, Johnson & Johnson expects to pay approximately $3 billion in 2027, with the remaining payments scheduled for 2028. headlines.title: Kamchatka’s Shiveluch spews ash 9 km high
headlines.full_text: Kamchatka’s Shiveluch spews ash 9 km high Shiveluch is the northernmost active volcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula MOSCOW, July 28. /TASS/. The Shiveluch volcano on Russia’s Far Eastern Kamchatka Peninsula has spewed ash to an altitude of nine kilometers above sea level, the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT) said. "According to seismic data, an ash plume from the Shiveluch volcano rose to an altitude of 9,000 meters above sea level," it wrote on messaging app Max. Shiveluch is the northernmost active volcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula. It is located 450 kilometers northeast of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky. The absolute height of the volcano is 3,283 meters. The highest point of its active part, called Young Shiveluch, is 2,500 meters above sea level, the diameter of the crater is 1.5 kilometers. Catastrophic eruptions took place in 1864 and 1964, when a large part of the lava dome collapsed and created a devastating debris avalanche. Young Shiveluch has been active since September 1980.
headlines.llm_reasoning: The article presents factual information about the volcanic eruption without emotional language or sensationalism, adhering to a neutral and objective tone.

headlines.full_text: Oil jumps over 3% as US crude stockpiles shrink, OPEC+ seen pausing output hikes Oil prices rose more than 3 per cent in early trade, with Brent climbing to $86.80 a barrel, after US crude inventories fell sharply and reports suggested OPEC+ may pause output increases from October, boosting supply concerns Oil prices climbed more than 3 per cent in early Asian trade on Wednesday, recovering a portion of the previous session’s sharp losses, after industry data showed a larger-than-expected decline in US crude inventories and reports suggested OPEC+ could pause planned production increases later this year. Brent crude futures rose $2.71, or 3.2 per cent, to $86.80 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained $2.26, or 3.4 per cent, to $81.95 a barrel. The rebound came a day after oil prices tumbled around 5 per cent to a two-week low, as hopes of renewed diplomacy between Washington and Tehran eased concerns over immediate supply disruptions linked to the conflict in West Asia. Supporting prices on Wednesday, US crude oil inventories fell by around 3.3 million barrels in the week ended July 24, according to reports citing data from the American Petroleum Institute (API). However, refined fuel inventories moved in the opposite direction. Gasoline stockpiles increased by about 918,000 barrels, while distillate inventories, which include diesel and heating oil, rose by roughly 355,000 barrels from the previous week. Investors will now await official inventory figures from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), due later on Wednesday, for confirmation of the API data.
